title: Lively v. Wild Oats Markets, Inc. (2006)
summary: The forum-defendant violation did not authorize the late remand because the defect was procedural and the objection period had passed.
notes:
Do not infer that parties can waive the absence of complete diversity or another genuine defect in subject-matter jurisdiction.

Lively sued in California state court over a slip and fall in a Wild Oats store; Wild Oats removed on diversity, no remand motion was filed within 30 days, and the Ninth Circuit held the forum-defendant rule is procedural and waivable and so cannot support a district court's sua sponte remand, joining eight of nine circuits to decide the question (456 F.3d 933).

sections.Parties: Lively sued Wild Oats. The dispute concerned removal of a diversity action in the face of the forum-defendant restriction.
sections.Material Facts: The action had an otherwise sufficient diversity basis, but removal violated the restriction associated with a defendant’s forum citizenship. The case remained in federal court for months before the remand issue was acted upon. The distinction between original jurisdiction and compliance with removal procedure determined whether the objection remained available.
sections.Procedural History: The Ninth Circuit rejected the late remand based on the procedural defect. The casebook identifies the passage of approximately eight months as important to the result.
sections.Issue: Was violation of the forum-defendant rule a subject-matter defect that could support remand at any time?
sections.Holding: No. It was a procedural removal defect subject to the statutory deadline for requesting remand on that ground.
sections.Reasoning: The presence of a forum defendant does not necessarily destroy the complete diversity on which original federal jurisdiction rests. Congress nevertheless restricts removal in that situation. Because those are different questions, the objection to removal could be forfeited even though a true absence of subject-matter jurisdiction could not. The case is a practical application of the distinction introduced by Lacks and Capron.

learning.why: The forum-defendant violation did not authorize the late remand because the defect was procedural and the objection period had passed.

topics.cp-forum-defendant: The forum-defendant restriction was treated as a procedural removal limit rather than a defect in subject-matter jurisdiction.
topics.cp-waiver: A procedural removal objection was subject to the statutory remand deadline.
topics.cp-removal: The case distinguishes jurisdictional removal defects from procedural ones subject to the 30-day remand motion deadline in 1447(c).
topics.cp-usc-1441: The decision construes the forum-defendant limitation in 1441(b) as non-jurisdictional.

mnemonic.rationale: A slip and fall, removed too late to complain
